text: Every superconducting qubit is a race against time: the quantum information it holds decays, and the clock that matters most is how much useful work can happen before it does. T1 and T2 are the two numbers that describe that clock.

T1, the energy relaxation time, measures how long a qubit prepared in the excited state takes, on average, to decay back down to the ground state — losing its energy to the surrounding environment. T2, the dephasing time, measures something different: how long a qubit prepared in a superposition maintains the precise phase relationship between its two components before noise scrambles it. A qubit can lose that phase information — becoming effectively a random mix of zero and one — even without losing any energy at all. In practice, both are measured directly on real hardware: T1 through a relaxation experiment, T2 through a Ramsey or spin-echo experiment.

T1 and T2 aren't independent. The standard relationship is one over T2 equals one over twice T1, plus one over the pure dephasing time, Tφ. Because that last term is always zero or positive, T2 can never exceed twice T1. Run the numbers for a qubit with T1 of 100 microseconds and a pure dephasing time of 100 microseconds, and you get T2 of about 66.7 microseconds — well under the 200-microsecond ceiling. T2 only approaches that 2-times-T1 limit when pure dephasing becomes negligible, and in practice some pure dephasing is essentially always present.

Every gate operation takes a finite amount of time, and every qubit — whether it's actively being used or just sitting idle — is decaying and dephasing the whole time. If a circuit's total run time becomes a significant fraction of T1 or T2, the chance of decoherence partway through becomes significant, and the final measurement becomes unreliable. That's why coherence time is often described as placing a hard ceiling on circuit depth. Coherence times have improved substantially across device generations — early superconducting qubits were measured in nanoseconds to low microseconds; more recent devices have reached tens to a few hundred microseconds, roughly. Treat any more specific number as a snapshot of one device at one point in time, not a stable industry figure.
